guides.title: Launch your first website for ₹0
guides.outcome: A live website at a real URL — free to host, free to update, forever.
guides.intro: You do not need a server, a credit card or a framework. One HTML file and a GitHub account is enough to go live on the open internet today.

steps.title: Create one HTML file
steps.detail: Make a folder, create index.html, and write a simple page: a heading, a paragraph, a link. Save. That is a real website — everything else is decoration.
steps.tip: Start with <!DOCTYPE html> and one <section>. Resist the urge to add a framework.

steps.title: Open it in your browser
steps.detail: Double-click the file. It renders locally. Congratulations — this exact file is what visitors will see.

steps.title: Push it to GitHub
steps.detail: Create a free account at github.com, create a new repository, and upload index.html (drag-and-drop works — no terminal needed).
steps.tip: Repository name matters if you use GitHub Pages: username.github.io becomes your URL.

steps.title: Turn on GitHub Pages
steps.detail: In the repo: Settings → Pages → deploy from main branch. Within a minute your site is live at https://username.github.io.

steps.title: Or deploy on Cloudflare Pages (unlimited bandwidth)
steps.detail: Connect the same GitHub repo at pages.cloudflare.com. You get a free SSL URL, unlimited bandwidth and automatic deploys on every change.

steps.title: Make your first change
steps.detail: Edit index.html, commit, refresh. Deploys are automatic. This loop — edit, commit, live — is the core skill of the whole web.
steps.tip: Add a footer: 'Built by hand, hosted for free.' Your first commit message should be 'first site'.

steps.title: Level up next
steps.detail: Add real content, a custom domain later (~$10/year, optional), then follow the portfolio guide on this site to make it impressive.

outgrow: Need forms or logins? See the $0 full-stack stack in the directory.
Custom domain: buy from any registrar or get a free .me for a year with the GitHub Student Pack.

guides.title: Build a portfolio that gets interviews
guides.outcome: A portfolio page recruiters can scan in 30 seconds, with proof of real work.
guides.intro: A portfolio is not a CV in HTML. It is evidence: three real projects, each with a live link and a story about the problem it solves.

steps.title: Write before you design
steps.detail: Draft in plain text: who you are (2 sentences), 3 projects (each: what it does, what you built, link), how to contact you. If the words are weak, design cannot save them.
steps.tip: Every project needs: 1 problem, 1 screenshot, 1 live link, 1 repo link.

steps.title: Pick a two-font, two-colour system
steps.detail: Choose a display font and body font from Google Fonts (free), and two colours from Coolors. Constraints force taste.

steps.title: Build three sections, nothing more
steps.detail: Hero (name + what you do), Projects (cards), Contact. Skip the skills bars and the animated timeline — recruiters skim, they do not read.

steps.title: Make the projects undeniable
steps.detail: For each project: one clear screenshot (compress with Squoosh), one sentence on the problem, one sentence on your solution, links to live demo + code.

steps.title: Add the boring trust signals
steps.detail: GitHub link, LinkedIn link, a real photo or avatar, and a plain email. No contact form for a first portfolio — it adds friction and looks like hiding.

steps.title: Ship it
steps.detail: Deploy with the 'first website' guide. Then share it: put the URL in your GitHub bio, LinkedIn, and every job application.

steps.title: Iterate on proof, not pixels
steps.detail: The biggest portfolio upgrade is always a better project — not a better animation. Ship something small and real every month.

outgrow: Add a blog to show you can write; add case studies when a project gets users.

guides.title: Start a blog for free — and keep it alive
guides.outcome: A fast blog you own, plus a writing habit that compounds.
guides.intro: The expensive part of blogging is not hosting — it is consistency. Set up something boringly simple and spend your energy on posts.

steps.title: Choose your lane
steps.detail: Pick 2-3 topics you can write about repeatedly without burning out (what you are learning counts — build-in-public posts are the easiest honest content).

steps.title: Simplest possible setup
steps.detail: Option A (zero code): publish on dev.to or Medium, free with built-in audience. Option B (you own it): a static site on GitHub Pages — one Markdown file per post with a tiny converter or a static site generator.

steps.title: Make the writing template
steps.detail: Every post: 1 promise in the title, 1 problem, your process, 1 result, 1 next step. Write the title last. 300 honest words beat 1500 padded ones.

steps.title: Publish before it is perfect
steps.detail: Ship post #1 this week. typos can be fixed in a commit; an empty blog fixes itself only by publishing.
steps.tip: Aim for one post per week for 8 weeks before judging results.

steps.title: Make it findable
steps.detail: Add clear titles and descriptions (search engines index static sites happily), and cross-post each article to dev.to with a canonical link back to your site.

steps.title: Track one metric only
steps.detail: Not visitors — published posts. Consistency is the metric you control; traffic follows it with a 2-3 month lag.

outgrow: Add a newsletter later with a free tier (e.g. Buttondown or Mailchimp free); add comments with giscus (runs on GitHub).

guides.title: Build your own AI chatbot — with $0 of API spend
guides.outcome: Your own chat UI answering questions, powered by free AI models.
guides.intro: You do not need a paid API key. Free tiers from Groq and Google AI Studio are generous enough to build and even run small products on — and running models locally with Ollama costs nothing at all.

steps.title: Get a free key
steps.detail: Sign up at Groq (fast open models like Llama, ~thousands of free requests/day) or Google AI Studio (free Gemini Flash access). Copy the API key.
steps.tip: Never put the key in frontend code — that is how keys get stolen.

steps.title: Build the chat UI
steps.detail: A single HTML page: input box, message list, fetch() call that streams the reply. Store conversation in an array and send it with each request for context.

steps.title: Hide the key behind a proxy
steps.detail: Deploy a tiny Cloudflare Worker that stores the key as an environment variable and forwards requests. 100,000 free requests/day is your rate limiter too.

steps.title: Add the system prompt
steps.detail: Give the model a personality and rules in one sentence at the top of the messages array ('You are a helpful assistant for X. Keep answers short.'). This one line changes everything.

steps.title: Deploy the frontend
steps.detail: Put the chat page on Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages, pointing at your Worker. Live chatbot, real URL, zero cost.

steps.title: Want unlimited + private? Go local
steps.detail: Install Ollama, run a small model (e.g. llama3.2 3B), point your UI at http://localhost:11434. Same code, no key, no limits — just your hardware.

outgrow: Add memory (store conversations in a free Supabase table), or RAG — see the 'chat with your notes' guide.

guides.title: Chat with your own notes (RAG, the free way)
guides.outcome: A tool that answers questions using your PDFs and notes — privately, for free.
guides.intro: RAG = retrieve relevant chunks of your documents, then let an LLM answer using them. The zero-code path takes 10 minutes; the build-it-yourself path teaches you the pattern behind every AI product.

steps.title: Try the zero-code version first
steps.detail: NotebookLM (Google, free) lets you upload sources and ask questions against them. Use it to understand what good RAG feels like before building one.

steps.title: Split documents into chunks
steps.detail: In Python: load text, cut into ~500-character chunks with slight overlap. Chunks are the unit of retrieval — too big and answers get vague, too small and context is lost.
steps.tip: Google Colab gives you a free GPU+CPU notebook to do all of this.

steps.title: Embed the chunks locally
steps.detail: Use sentence-transformers or fastembed — free, runs on CPU, no API. Each chunk becomes a vector; store them in Chroma (embedded, no server).

steps.title: Retrieve, then answer
steps.detail: On each question: embed the question, find the 5 nearest chunks, paste them into the prompt, and send to a free LLM (Groq or local Ollama). Ask the model to answer only from the provided context.

steps.title: Show your sources
steps.detail: Print which chunks the answer came from. Trustworthy RAG always cites — this also makes bugs obvious fast.

steps.title: Wrap it in an interface
steps.detail: A simple Streamlit or plain HTML page over the same logic. Now you have a private, free, source-cited research assistant for your own documents.

outgrow: More documents → Qdrant or pgvector on a free tier; better retrieval → try hybrid search (keywords + vectors).

guides.title: The free AI image toolkit (generate → edit → upscale → publish)
guides.outcome: A complete free workflow for AI images — and a clear conscience about licences.
guides.intro: You can do the full image pipeline without paying: generate free, edit free, upscale free, compress free. The only real skill is knowing which tool for which job — and what you are allowed to use commercially.

steps.title: Generate: pick your free generator
steps.detail: Google ImageFX and Microsoft's Bing Image Creator give free daily generations of the big models. For text-in-images, Ideogram's free tier leads. Save all good prompts in a text file — prompts are reusable assets.

steps.title: Edit: Photopea is the free Photoshop
steps.detail: Photopea runs in the browser, opens PSD files, handles layers and is free with ads. Crop, retouch, compose — no install.

steps.title: Upscale: Upscayl, locally
steps.detail: Upscayl is open-source and runs on your machine — 4x upscaling with real models, no upload of your images.

steps.title: Compress before publishing
steps.detail: Squoosh (Google, browser-based) cuts file size 5-10x with negligible quality loss. Page speed is an image-weight problem 90% of the time.

steps.title: Know the licence
steps.detail: Check each tool's terms for commercial use — most allow it, some restrict. When in doubt, generate your own rather than reposting, and never generate real people's likenesses.
steps.tip: For unlimited generation and full control, run ComfyUI or Fooocus locally — free, open-source, your GPU.

steps.title: Build a prompt library
steps.detail: Keep a growing doc of prompts that worked, per style. After 20 generations you will write better prompts than 90% of tutorials.

outgrow: Batch workflows → ComfyUI graphs; brand consistency → train a small LoRA on Colab's free GPU.

guides.title: Start a faceless YouTube channel with free tools
guides.outcome: Your first published video — no face, no camera, no spend.
guides.intro: Faceless channels work because the value is the script and the edit, not your face. Everything below is free-tier or open-source; the honest catch: monetization takes months, so pick a topic you actually enjoy.

steps.title: Pick a niche you can sustain
steps.detail: Explainers, history, tech breakdowns, finance basics — choose something you can script weekly without research fatigue. Channel value = repeatable format.
steps.tip: Watch 5 top channels in your niche and write down their video formula.

steps.title: Script with a free chatbot
steps.detail: Use ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini free tiers to outline and draft — but rewrite every sentence in your own voice. Raw AI voice is the #1 reason faceless channels die.
steps.tip: Prompt pattern: 'Explain X to a curious beginner. 8 short sections, each with one concrete example.'

steps.title: Voiceover: free tiers exist
steps.detail: ElevenLabs free tier gives ~10 minutes/month of very natural TTS — enough for testing formats. For unlimited: record yourself (free, faster than you think) or use open-source TTS like Piper/Kokoro.

steps.title: Visuals: stock + screenshots + motion
steps.detail: Free stock footage (Pexels/Pixabay), screen recordings with OBS, and simple animated text in CapCut. One visual change every 5-8 seconds keeps retention.

steps.title: Edit in CapCut (free)
steps.detail: CapCut desktop is free and handles captions, zooms, transitions. Learn 3 things only: captions, cut-to-breath, and text-on-screen. That is 80% of faceless editing.

steps.title: Thumbnail + title decide everything
steps.detail: Make the thumbnail in Canva free: 3 words max, one focal face/object, high contrast. The title makes a promise the thumbnail visualizes.

steps.title: Publish 10 before judging
steps.detail: Upload weekly. Study which topics get clicked (CTR) vs watched (retention). Video #10 will embarrass video #1 — that is the plan working.

outgrow: Consistency proven → upgrade voiceover to paid TTS; repurpose every video into Shorts and a blog post.

guides.title: Launch a podcast for exactly ₹0
guides.outcome: Your podcast on Spotify and Apple Podcasts via RSS — zero hosting fees.
guides.intro: Podcast 'hosting' sounds expensive and is not: Spotify for Podcasters (formerly Anchor) hosts unlimited audio free and pushes your RSS feed everywhere. Spend your budget on a quiet room instead.

steps.title: Record in the quietest room you have
steps.detail: Your phone + earphones mic is good enough to start. Record 10cm from the mic, in a room with soft stuff (beds, curtains) to kill echo.
steps.tip: The blanket-fort recording booth is a real technique, not a joke.

steps.title: Edit in Audacity
steps.detail: Free, open-source, forever. Learn three edits: cut mistakes, cut silence, normalize volume. That is all a podcast edit is.

steps.title: Clean up voice with free AI
steps.detail: Adobe Podcast's free enhance removes room noise frighteningly well; Auphonic gives free monthly hours of automatic leveling and loudness. One or the other — not both.

steps.title: Cover art + description
steps.detail: 3000x3000px cover (Canva free), title under 3 words per idea, one-sentence description with the words people actually search for.

steps.title: Upload to Spotify for Podcasters
steps.detail: Free hosting, automatic distribution to Spotify, and an RSS feed you submit to Apple Podcasts and others. Unlimited episodes, zero cost.

steps.title: Ship 5 episodes before promoting
steps.detail: Listeners binge — a podcast with 5 episodes gets subscribed; one with 1 gets sampled. Batch-record 3 in one sitting.

outgrow: Video podcast → OBS recording + CapCut; transcripts → Whisper (free, local) improves SEO and accessibility.

guides.title: Automate your life with free workflows (n8n + cron)
guides.outcome: Real automations running 24/7 — file sorting, digests, alerts — for free.
guides.intro: Zapier's free tier is a teaser. The honest free path is either self-hosting n8n (unlimited automations on hardware you own) or abusing GitHub Actions cron — both genuinely free.

steps.title: List 5 things you do repeatedly
steps.detail: Examples: daily news digest to Telegram, rename + file screenshots, backup a folder weekly, track prices, remind yourself of things. Automation only pays off on repeated tasks.
steps.tip: Start with one that annoys you weekly, not monthly.

steps.title: Pick your engine
steps.detail: n8n self-hosted: visual workflows, 400+ integrations, free unlimited on your machine. GitHub Actions cron: free for public repos, perfect for script-y tasks on a schedule.

steps.title: Self-host n8n with Docker
steps.detail: One docker command runs n8n on an old laptop, a Raspberry Pi, or an Oracle Cloud free-tier VM (4 ARM cores, free forever). Access it privately via Tailscale.

steps.title: Build your first workflow
steps.detail: Trigger (schedule) → fetch (RSS/weather/API) → format (function node) → notify (Telegram bot or email via Resend free tier). One afternoon, one working automation.

steps.title: Add a Telegram bot as your control panel
steps.detail: Bots are free: message your server commands, get digests back. Telegram's Bot API needs no payment setup at all.

steps.title: Make failures loud
steps.detail: Add an error branch that pings you when a workflow fails. Silent automation failures are worse than no automation.
steps.tip: Rule: every automation either logs visibly or messages you. No exceptions.

outgrow: More uptime → Oracle free VM or a cheap VPS; more brains → add an LLM step with Groq's free tier.

guides.title: Learn Python in 30 days — the free curriculum
guides.outcome: From zero to writing useful scripts confidently, with a portfolio of small programs.
guides.intro: Every resource in this plan is free. The scarce resource is your hour a day — the plan protects it: learn 20 minutes, code 40 minutes, ship something tiny every week.

steps.title: Day 1: Install and print
steps.detail: Install Python from python.org + VS Code with the Python extension. First program: input → compute → print. Type every character yourself — no copy-paste for 30 days.

steps.title: Days 2-7: Core syntax, daily reps
steps.detail: Variables, if/else, loops, lists, dicts, functions. Do freeCodeCamp's Scientific Computing course or Kaggle's Python course — pick one, finish it.

steps.title: Week 1 project: a money calculator
steps.detail: Split-the-bill + tip calculator with input validation. Ugly is fine. Working is required. Push it to GitHub — repo #1.
steps.tip: Every week ends with a shipped mini-project. This is the whole method.

steps.title: Days 8-14: Files and errors
steps.detail: Read/write files, CSVs, try/except, command-line arguments. Week 2 project: a to-do list that saves to a file between runs.

steps.title: Days 15-21: The standard library superpower
steps.detail: requests (download a webpage), datetime, json. Week 3 project: a weather notifier — fetch a free API (Open-Meteo, no key needed) and print/notify.

steps.title: Days 22-30: Pick a direction
steps.detail: Automate boring files (os, shutil) OR data analysis (pandas on Kaggle) OR web scraping (requests + BeautifulSoup). Week 4 project: automate one real thing in your own life.

steps.title: Keep the reps going
steps.detail: After day 30: 2-3 Exercism exercises weekly for precision, easy LeetCode for interviews, and one growing real project. Free forever — the hour was the only cost.

outgrow: Direction chosen → the AI Engineer or Software Developer roadmaps on roadmap.sh, mapped to free resources in the learning directory.

guides.title: Self-hosting 101: your own private cloud from junk hardware
guides.outcome: An old PC running your files, photos and apps — private, free, yours.
guides.intro: Any machine with 4GB RAM can become a private cloud. The stack is always the same: Linux → Docker → apps → private access. Free, no subscriptions, your data never leaves the house unless you say so.

steps.title: Pick the machine
steps.detail: Old laptop (best: built-in UPS battery), mini-PC, or Raspberry Pi. Wired ethernet > wifi. Any 4GB+ RAM machine is enough for files, photos and a dozen small apps.

steps.title: Install Ubuntu Server
steps.detail: Free OS, installs in 20 minutes from a USB stick. Enable SSH. Update it. This machine now lives in a corner and is controlled from your main computer.

steps.title: Docker is the app store
steps.detail: Install Docker, then run apps as containers: Nextcloud (files), PhotoPrism/Immich (photos), Jellyfin (media). One YAML file per app = clean installs, clean removals.

steps.title: Access from anywhere: Tailscale, not port-forwarding
steps.detail: Install Tailscale on the server and your devices — private mesh network, no open ports, no exposed router, free for personal use. This single step removes 90% of self-hosting risk.

steps.title: Backups or it did not happen
steps.detail: 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite. Automate with Duplicati or Kopia to an external drive + free cloud storage. Test a restore once — untested backups are hopes, not backups.

steps.title: Power + monitoring reality check
steps.detail: An old laptop draws ~10W ≈ one LED bulb. Enable auto-restart after outages, and set UptimeRobot (free) to ping your services so you know when something dies.
steps.tip: If your electricity is unreliable, self-host the non-critical stuff and keep critical files in two places.

outgrow: One-click app management → Coolify; public-facing services → Cloudflare Tunnel; heavier apps → Oracle free-tier ARM VM as a second node.

guides.title: Get freelance-ready with free tools (any country)
guides.outcome: The complete free infrastructure for taking your first paid work: presence, proposals, contracts, invoices, payments.
guides.intro: Freelancing has a tooling problem only for people who buy tools. This guide assembles the entire stack for $0 — and points you to the payment rails that actually work in your country.

steps.title: One page that sells you
steps.detail: Portfolio with 2-3 real things (the portfolio guide covers this). Add a 'Services' section: 3 specific offers with prices. Specific beats general every time.
steps.tip: Offer template: 'I build X for Y so that Z' + price range + 2-week delivery.

steps.title: Book calls without back-and-forth
steps.detail: Cal.com (open-source) or Calendly free: one link, people pick a slot. Add a 15-minute 'scoping call' — shorter calls close faster.

steps.title: Track leads in a free workspace
steps.detail: Notion or Trello free: one board, columns = Lead → Replied → Call → Proposal → Won/Lost. The freelance winners are usually just the ones who followed up.

steps.title: Proposals that close
steps.detail: One page: their problem in their words, your plan in 5 bullets, price with two options (good/better), start date. Send within 24h of the call while it is fresh.
steps.tip: Take 30-50% upfront, always. Free tools do not pay for scope creep — deposits do.

steps.title: Contracts: simple and written
steps.detail: A plain-language one-pager beats nothing: scope, price, timeline, 2 revision rounds, payment terms. Templates exist free (search 'freelance contract template') — read before you sign anything.

steps.title: Get paid: pick your rails
steps.detail: Open the World page on this site — it maps working payment rails per country (Stripe/PayPal where available, Payoneer/Wise for payouts, local options elsewhere). Set up before your first client, not after.

steps.title: First clients: cold and warm
steps.detail: Warm: tell your network exactly what you now offer (most first gigs come from people who already know you). Cold: 5 personalized messages a day to businesses with visible problems you fix.

outgrow: Taxes: track every invoice in a spreadsheet from day one; local registration rules vary — check your country's threshold before scaling.
